work-energy-theorem.title: Work-Energy Theorem
work-energy-theorem.conceptual_definition: The Work-Energy Theorem states that the net work $W$ done by all forces acting on an object is equal to the change in the object's kinetic energy $\Delta T$.
work-energy-theorem.intuitive_summary: This theorem quantifies how much an object's motion (kinetic energy) changes due to the total effort (work) exerted on it, establishing work as a transfer of energy.
work-energy-theorem.interpretation: The Work-Energy Theorem is a fundamental principle in classical mechanics, providing a powerful tool for analyzing the motion of particles and rigid bodies. It establishes a direct relationship between the work $W$ done by the net force $\mathbf{F}$ on a particle along a path $C$ and the resulting change in its kinetic energy $T$. The equation $W = \int_{C} \mathbf{F} \cdot d\mathbf{r}$ defines the work done, which, through the application of Newton's second law $\mathbf{F} = m \frac{d\mathbf{v}}{dt}$ and kinematic relations, can be shown to be equivalent to the change in the quantity $\frac{1}{2} m v^2$. This quantity is defined as the kinetic energy $T$. Thus, $W = \Delta T$. This theorem is particularly useful in situations where forces are variable or paths are complex, as it often simplifies problem-solving by avoiding direct integration of acceleration to find velocity and displacement.
work-energy-theorem.symmetry_origin: The Work-Energy Theorem is a direct consequence of Newton's second law of motion and the definitions of work and kinetic energy. While not directly derived from a continuous symmetry via Noether's theorem, it is deeply connected to the underlying principles of energy conservation. For conservative forces, the work done can be expressed as the negative change in potential energy, leading to the conservation of total mechanical energy, which is a consequence of time-translation invariance. For non-conservative forces, the work done by these forces accounts for the change in mechanical energy, upholding the broader principle of energy conservation.
work-energy-theorem.limits_and_boundary: This theorem is valid within the framework of classical mechanics, specifically in the non-relativistic limit where particle speeds $v$ are much less than the speed of light $c$. It applies to point particles or rigid bodies undergoing translational motion. For systems with internal degrees of freedom or deformation, the work done might also contribute to changes in internal energy. In the absence of non-conservative forces, the work done by conservative forces is equal to the negative change in potential energy, $W_c = -\Delta U$, leading to the conservation of total mechanical energy $E = T + U = \text{constant}$.

W.name: Work Done
W.description: The net work done by all forces acting on the object.

F.name: Net Force
F.description: The vector sum of all external forces acting on the object.

dr.name: Infinitesimal Displacement Vector
dr.description: An infinitesimal vector representing the displacement along the path of motion.

C.name: Path of Integration
C.description: The specific path or trajectory along which the work is calculated.

t_1.name: Initial Time
t_1.description: The starting time of the motion.

t_2.name: Final Time
t_2.description: The ending time of the motion.

dv_dt.name: Acceleration Vector
dv_dt.description: The time derivative of the velocity vector, representing the acceleration of the object.

v.name: Velocity Vector
v.description: The instantaneous velocity vector of the object.

v_magnitude.name: Speed
v_magnitude.description: The magnitude of the velocity vector.

v_1.name: Initial Speed
v_1.description: The initial magnitude of the velocity of the object.

v_2.name: Final Speed
v_2.description: The final magnitude of the velocity of the object.

T.name: Kinetic Energy
T.description: The energy possessed by an object due to its motion, defined as \frac{1}{2}$mv^2$.

Delta_T.name: Change in Kinetic Energy
Delta_T.description: The difference between the final and initial kinetic energies of the object, $T_2 - T_1$.
